statement: The system shall provide astronomers with one integrated environment for controlling the telescope and instruments.
The system shall enable observers to acquire data efficiently.
The system shall enable observers to understand what the system is doing.
The system shall enable observers to judge data quality quickly while observing.
The system shall allow the right people to carry out their observing tasks smoothly from the appropriate local or remote facility.
The system shall provide consistent access to telescope status and observing functions.
The system shall enable observers to get reliable data.
The system shall enable observers to react quickly when conditions or instrument settings change.
The system shall enable observers to assess whether data are usable without a lot of manual coordination.
The system shall support observing astronomers as a main user group.
The system shall support telescope operators as a main user group.
The system shall support instrument or facility support staff as a main user group.
The system shall provide access from remote observing locations for some users.
The system shall allow observing astronomers to control their observations.
The system shall allow observing astronomers to control instrument settings.
The system shall allow observing astronomers to review data quality.
The system shall provide telescope operators with broader oversight of telescope status and day-to-day execution.
The system shall provide support staff with access to diagnostics.
The system shall provide support staff with access to configuration information.
The system shall provide support staff with access to status information.
The system shall not give support staff the same operational control as the primary observer.
Only the person or role responsible for the current observation shall be able to change telescope or instrument settings.
Access to change telescope or instrument settings shall be tied to the current session and operational authority, not just to a logged-in account.
The system shall track the observation itself, the active target, instrument configuration, telescope status, and resulting data products.
The system shall store enough metadata with resulting data products to know how they were acquired.
Status visibility shall be consistent so that local and remote users see the same operational picture.
Control transfer between locations shall be clean and auditable.
Any transfer of operational authority shall be explicit so that everyone knows who is in charge.
When operational authority changes, the previous controller may still view status and data if the previous controller's role allows it.
The telescope control system shall support astronomers and operators in controlling the telescopes.
The telescope control system shall allow astronomers and operators to access instrument status.
The telescope control system shall allow astronomers and operators to evaluate data quality from the right local or remote facilities.
The current system is fragmented.
The current process requires a fair amount of operator involvement.
The remote access experience is workable but inconsistent.
A more unified environment is desired.
The system shall reduce the need for astronomers to deal with low-level control details.
The system shall provide a single environment that integrates telescope status, instrument control, data acquisition, and quick assessment of data quality.
The system shall provide consistent access for users whether they are on-site or working from an approved remote facility.
The system should reflect different user responsibilities so that users only see and do what matches their operational role.
The system shall support straightforward observing workflows.
The system shall provide clear alarm or exception handling so operators can respond quickly when something is off.
The system shall allow astronomers to collect scientifically useful data from the telescope without dealing with the mechanics of the instruments and control subsystems.
The system shall improve observing efficiency.
The system shall help ensure that telescope time produces high-quality results.
The system shall provide the observing team with a single, reliable way to point the telescope, configure the system, monitor the observation, and assess the observation as it happens.
The system shall allow the observing team to determine whether the telescope and instruments are behaving correctly.
The system shall allow the observing team to judge data quality quickly.
The system shall allow the observing team to adjust the plan when conditions or results are not meeting expectations.
The system shall produce usable scientific results from the observing session.
The observation shall be executed safely.
The correct instrument setup shall be achieved.
The astronomer shall be able to confirm that the intended target was completed.
The astronomer shall be able to confirm that the exposure sequence was completed.
The system shall support quick recovery or adjustment when conditions change.
The system shall provide accurate telescope control.
The system shall provide reliable instrument configuration.

The system shall ensure that failures in accurate telescope control, reliable instrument configuration, or real-time status and quality feedback do not cause the night to be lost or the data to become unusable.
The system shall support quick adaptation to changing conditions.
The system shall keep the observer workflow simple to avoid wasting time on operational complexity.
The system shall include convenience features as lower-priority capabilities than safety, correctness, and steady observing throughput.
The system shall prioritize safety over convenience features.
The system shall support quick switching between targets or observing modes during an observing session.
The system shall handle complex instrument setups without error-prone operation.
The system shall ensure that a previous configuration is fully cleared before a new configuration is applied.
The system shall allow the team to react quickly to changes in weather, seeing, or tracking conditions while avoiding mistakes.
The system shall minimize delay and configuration errors when users must manage several subsystems manually at the same time.
The observer shall be hidden from individual device protocols.
The observer shall be hidden from the separate steps needed to move motors.
The system shall provide a single observing interface that presents the telescope and instruments in terms of what the observer wants to do rather than how the hardware happens to do it.
Usually the observing astronomer decides what the next observing action should be.
The system enforces a safe and valid sequence of steps.
When the observing sequence has to be adjusted quickly, the instrument specialist shall help interpret whether the change is feasible.
When the observing sequence has to be adjusted quickly, the instrument specialist shall help determine whether the resulting data will still be scientifically valid.
The instrument specialist shall troubleshoot instrument-specific issues faster than the observing astronomer or general operator.
The system shall support shared understanding of pause.
The system shall support shared understanding of abort.
The system shall support shared understanding of recover.
Readiness means the telescope and instrument are fully in a safe, configured state.
If someone tries to use readiness, pause, abort, or recover in an unexpected state, the system shall refuse the action.
The system shall confirm that the telescope and instrument are in a known safe state before proceeding with setup.
The system shall slew to the target.
The system shall either continue with the next target or wrap up the session and stow the system safely after the quality review.
The system shall have clear operational criteria for determining session start and end.
If the required conditions are not fully met, the system shall not mark the session as started or ended.
A change in tracking drift conditions shall be treated as a main trigger for system action.
When triggering events occur, the system should respond automatically where possible by moving to the next safe step.
When triggering events occur and automatic response is not possible, the system should present a clear status and require operator confirmation.
Each event should cause the system to execute the observing action, pause the observing action, or protect the hardware and data quality if the situation is no longer acceptable.
Manual changes should be limited to the people responsible for the relevant subsystem.
The instrument specialist should handle instrument settings, and the telescope operator should handle telescope-related adjustments.
The order of manual changes should follow the dependency chain.
Safety and basic configuration should be performed first.
Pointing and instrument setup should be performed after safety and basic configuration.
The observing action itself should be performed only after pointing and instrument setup.
The system should stop and ask for confirmation whenever a change could affect safety.
The system should stop and ask for confirmation whenever a change could invalidate the current configuration.
The system should stop and ask for confirmation whenever a change could introduce a delay that might make the sequence inconsistent with the planned observation.
A manual change may proceed without confirmation only when it is clearly low risk, reversible, and does not affect the current exposure, telescope motion, or instrument state in any meaningful way.
An acceptable override is usually a correction to a minor display or metadata issue.
An acceptable override is usually a pre-approved tweak that the current operator role is explicitly allowed to perform.
If a manual change could alter the observing result, interfere with safety, or break the planned sequence, it must require a stop and confirmation.
The system shall produce associated calibration frames.
The system shall produce basic metadata describing how each exposure was taken.
The system shall preserve the produced data products so astronomers can verify the observation, compare it against the intended setup, and later pass it into reduction or archive processes.
The system shall automatically capture the data products during observing and make them available quickly enough for the team to decide whether to continue, repeat, or adjust the next observation.
The responsibility for making a manual subsystem change may shift only under controlled conditions.
The subsystem owner or designated operator normally makes the change.
If the subsystem owner or designated operator is unavailable or the observation is time-critical, a qualified backup role may make the change if the backup has proper access.
When a qualified backup role makes the change, the role shift must be recorded for accountability.
If the backup is not explicitly authorized, the system shall hold the change and require escalation instead of allowing informal action by another person.
A later step may proceed if the system can safely and explicitly validate the dependency at that time.
If the prerequisite cannot be satisfied without risking the observing window or configuration integrity, the system shall block the change and escalate to the operator.
The system shall allow a manual override without confirmation only for minor, low-risk adjustments that do not affect the active exposure or hardware motion.
The system shall allow a manual override without confirmation for correcting a non-operational setting.
The system shall allow a manual override without confirmation for fixing a labeling error.
The system shall allow a manual override without confirmation for applying a pre-approved housekeeping change.
The system shall stop and require operator approval whenever there is any doubt about the impact of a change.
Remotely operated sessions shall be more conservative because there is less immediate physical oversight.
If staffing is reduced or on-site response is delayed, the system shall limit manual changes to pre-authorized actions.
If staffing is reduced or on-site response is delayed, the system shall prefer automated safeguards or deferred execution rather than allowing operators to force risky adjustments.
If direct oversight is lost altogether, the system shall block any nonessential change until communication and authority are restored.
If a request can be translated safely and unambiguously, the system shall handle the low-level steps automatically so the observer does not have to manage subsystem details.
If a request is ambiguous, risky, or requires judgment about the telescope or instrument state, the system shall route it to an operator rather than reject it outright.
If a request cannot be mapped to a valid observing operation at all, the system shall reject it as too technical.
The observing sequence should be deferred if the fix would consume more time than the current observing slot can tolerate.
The observing sequence should resume only after the state is confirmed healthy and the operator agrees that the next step is safe to continue.
The system shall define warning thresholds for unstable tracking.
The system shall define warning thresholds for instrument status faults.
The system shall define warning thresholds for configuration mismatches.
The system shall automatically pause before the next step when unstable tracking, instrument status faults, or a configuration mismatch occur.
If a condition is borderline rather than outright failed, the system shall warn the operator and require operator approval before continuing.
The system shall treat any hardware safety issue as a hard stop until it is cleared.

The observatory software and operations support team should work closely with instrument specialists and operators who know the subsystem details when maintaining and updating the control environment.
If a new telescope setup fits the same basic observing pattern and only changes parameters, mappings, or supported limits, the control system should handle it with a configuration update.

If a new telescope setup changes how observers acquire targets, manage exposures, switch instruments, or check quality in a meaningful way, the control system should require a more substantial workflow change.
Any change that affects the operator handoff, approvals, or safety checks should be treated as a workflow change rather than as a configuration tweak.
If a service is slow or returns an error, the interface shall present a clear operational state and the next safe option.
If a service is slow or returns an error, the interface shall not expose raw technical noise.
A change shall wait until the night is safe if it could interrupt an active exposure.
A contained update that has already been tested and only requires a planned switch-over with no impact on active work can be enabled sooner in a controlled window.
The deciding factor is whether a change can be made without risking the current session or forcing operators into an unplanned recovery.

A new telescope configuration or instrument shall be introduced as a plug-in extension if it can use the same observing steps, status model, and operator controls with only added parameters or device-specific translations.

A new telescope configuration or instrument shall require a dedicated adaptation if it introduces a different sequence of actions, new timing constraints, or a different way of assessing data quality.
The system shall preserve a consistent observing workflow for astronomers and operators while allowing the subsystem to behave correctly.
A subsystem interface shall be treated as a dedicated adaptation if it requires its own safety interlocks.
A subsystem interface shall be treated as a dedicated adaptation if it requires a different command sequence.
A subsystem interface shall be treated as a dedicated adaptation if it requires special handling for failures that does not match the standard telescope and instrument flow.
A subsystem interface shall be treated as a dedicated adaptation if it involves long-running asynchronous actions.
A subsystem interface shall be treated as a dedicated adaptation if it involves multiple concurrent states.
A subsystem interface shall be treated as a dedicated adaptation if it can partially succeed and leave the system in an ambiguous condition.
A subsystem interface shall be treated as more than a plug-in if operators have to think about it differently to use it safely.
The system shall restrict some data when it could expose sensitive operational details, including proprietary observing programs and access-limited engineering information.
In live operations, observers shall be able to see the data and status they need for the current session.
In live operations, the system shall mask data that belongs to another program or to restricted technical diagnostics unless the user is authorized to view it.
If there is a security concern or a proprietary period, the system may delay or conceal the data.
A session shall start only when the needed authorization is in place.
Readiness checks for a session shall include telescope status, instrument status, and safety status.
A session shall be allowed to end for an approved handoff.
The system shall record status changes that involve a handoff between operators or sessions.
The system does not need to record every transition for routine internal churn if the transition does not change what the operator sees or does.
The system shall capture transitions that change the active target or observing mode.
The system shall capture transitions that explain why a slew or offset was commanded.
By default, users shall see only the current program’s information.
Cross-program data shall only appear if the user’s role explicitly requires it and the user is cleared for that level of access.
Deeper diagnostics shall only appear if the user’s role explicitly requires it and the user is cleared for that level of access.
Partially restricted details shall only appear if the user’s role explicitly requires it and the user is cleared for that level of access.
If there is any doubt about whether information should be shown, the system shall hide it.
Controls should stay as consistent as possible throughout the system.
If the same action appears in different functions, users should not have to relearn what it means or worry that it behaves differently unless there is a very clear operational reason.
Permitted exceptions to control consistency should be limited to clear operational reasons such as safety interlocks or role restrictions.
Any exception to control consistency should be rare and explicit.
The telescope control environment should avoid inconsistency because it can easily cause mistakes.
If the required state is not met, the system shall block the request outright and tell the user why.
The system shall use queuing only when the operation is explicitly designed to wait for a later state and that behavior has been agreed to be safe and predictable.
The system shall avoid allowing a request with only a warning unless the action is very low-impact.
For remote observing, feedback shall feel near real-time to the operator in order for the operator to trust it.
For remote observing, the system shall provide near real-time feedback for motion-related information.
For remote observing, the system shall provide near real-time feedback for exposure state information.
For remote observing, the system shall provide near real-time feedback for safety-related conditions.
If feedback delay exceeds a couple of seconds, it shall become difficult to make good decisions and to tell whether a command actually took effect.
For less critical status updates, the system may tolerate more delay.
The core control loop shall remain very responsive.
The system shall preserve useful auxiliary products such as quick-look quality assessments.
The system shall preserve useful auxiliary products such as reduced previews.
The system shall preserve useful auxiliary products such as acquisition images.
The system shall preserve useful auxiliary products such as session logs.
The system shall preserve auxiliary products when they help explain what happened or support later review.
The system shall discard items that are purely transient and not useful for science.
The system shall discard items that are purely transient and not useful for troubleshooting.
The system shall discard items that are purely transient and not useful for audit purposes.
The system shall keep a derived product if it is used to make an operational decision.
The system shall keep a derived product if it is used to document the state of the session.
A product shall be part of the official record if it is needed to reconstruct the observation.
A product shall be part of the official record if it is needed to support data quality review.
A product shall be part of the official record if it is needed to document a decision made during the session.
Telescope operations are currently split across many specialized controls and interfaces.
The system shall provide a single integrated environment for astronomers and operators to control the telescope and instruments.
The system shall allow users to monitor status.
The system shall allow users to judge data quality without juggling low-level subsystem details.
The system shall work cleanly for people in different roles.
The system shall support remote access where that is appropriate.
The system shall still leave enough control for the people who need it.
Exact numeric success targets need to be defined with the operations team.
The system shall make the handoff obvious so that stakeholders know whether the telescope, instrument, or data quality check is the immediate priority.
The system shall support clear task ownership and acknowledgements.
The system shall provide alerting or an event feed for urgent issues.
The system shall keep alerts or the event feed focused so that it does not become noise during the night.
When a fault occurs, the system should immediately surface what failed.
When a fault occurs, the system should indicate whether the telescope can safely continue or must pause.
The system should provide a clear recovery workflow that captures the incident.
The system should avoid requiring ad hoc coordination over radio or email for incident handling.
The system shall act as the single source of truth for session state.
The system shall automatically push important session state changes to the appropriate roles.
Each handoff shall include a timestamp.
The system shall provide a lightweight event timeline or activity feed.
The system shall raise the fault with a plain-language summary.
The responsible user shall be able to acknowledge the incident.
The system shall manage observing programs.
During observations, the system shall update telescope state and instrument state in real time.
When the session ends, the system shall archive the final state, logs, and data products together.
When the session ends, the system shall close out temporary operational records or retain them only as long as needed for audit and troubleshooting.
The system should use a structured model for the key data entities.
The system should avoid making the data model so fine-grained that it becomes hard to use in the middle of the night.
An observation sequence should include clear steps and parameters.
The system should be able to recover from interruptions in an observation sequence.
Faults and tasks should include severity information.
Faults and tasks should include ownership information.
Faults and tasks should include timestamps.
Faults and tasks should include current status information.
The level of structure should help operators and astronomers understand what is happening quickly.
The level of structure should give specialists the detail they need to diagnose problems without digging through unstructured notes.
The system shall present a clean view of what the telescope is doing.
During routine work, the system shall provide guided actions.
During routine work, the system shall provide guardrails so users can trigger the right operation without accidentally skipping a prerequisite or applying the wrong configuration.
During faults, the interface shall switch to a more focused recovery view.
During faults, the recovery view shall show a clear record of what has already been tried.
The system shall automatically assign a single owner to the recovery workflow or allow the operator to claim ownership.
The system shall present the approved recovery steps in order.
The system shall require confirmations before risky recovery steps are executed.
The system shall keep the session context attached to the incident.
The system shall allow the next person to continue the recovery task without starting over if the task is handed off or interrupted.
The system shall not show the same default level of detail to all users; it shall vary the level of detail by role for telescope operators, astronomers, and maintenance engineers.
The system shall surface only the controls and alerts relevant to each user role.
The system shall become more streamlined during routine stable periods.
The system shall become more explicit during faults or high-risk transitions.
The system shall provide enough context without overwhelming users.
The software shall be compatible with existing observatory hardware and control subsystems.
The software shall work within the established telescope safety interlocks.
The software shall work within the existing instrument interfaces.
The software shall work within site network limitations.
The software shall support both local observing and remote observing.
The software shall respect access controls during observing sessions.
The software shall follow procedures that keep the telescope safe during active sessions.
The system shall respect hardware handshakes.
The system shall avoid unsafe operations when the telescope is in an unsettled or protected state.
The system shall be responsive enough to support time-sensitive actions during exposures and target changes.
The system shall avoid delays that would disrupt observing.
The Gemini Telescope Control System shall coordinate tightly with telescope motion control.
Telescope motion control, instrument controllers, and the safety and enclosure systems determine whether an observation can proceed.
The software shall follow the subsystems' acknowledgment procedures closely.
The observatory control system shall tolerate heterogeneous response behavior across legacy and newer subsystems.
The observatory control system shall tolerate intermittent delays.
The observatory control system shall tolerate partial failures.
The observatory control system shall handle differences in status reporting without making the operator guess what really happened.
The observatory control system shall treat engaged safety interlocks as authoritative.
The Gemini Telescope Control System must comply with observatory safety policies and operational procedures.
The Gemini Telescope Control System must comply with observatory requirements for equipment protection.
The Gemini Telescope Control System must comply with observatory requirements for controlled access.
The Gemini Telescope Control System must support auditability.
The Gemini Telescope Control System must support safe shutdown behavior.
The control software shall be resilient to delayed or incomplete status updates from different observatory subsystems.
The system shall fail conservatively and make its state very explicit.
When appropriate, the system shall retry after a missing or inconsistent subsystem response.
If a problem affects safety or observation integrity, the system shall perform a controlled halt or rollback to the last known safe state.
For actions involving motion, power, or interlocks, the system shall prioritize protecting the telescope and instrument before preserving the observing sequence.
The system shall record who performed each action, when it was performed, and from where it was performed.
Sensitive actions that require approval include slews, instrument changes, and shutdowns.
The system shall support deliberate interactions rather than fast, implicit ones.
The interface shall show the exact effect of a command before it is executed.
A control handoff shall be triggered by the observing plan.
A control handoff shall be triggered by a shift change.
A control handoff shall be triggered when an operator takes over for a problem.
A control handoff shall be triggered when a remote observer passes control back to the on-site team.
When multiple users want to act at the same time, the system shall allow other users to observe or make suggestions without executing conflicting actions.
Data conversion must preserve configuration.
Data conversion must preserve logs.
Data conversion must preserve any operational records that are still needed.
The extent to which legacy data is migrated versus archived separately is undecided.
A clear support window is needed to keep the observatory operational while the new system proves itself.
Data mismatches are a main migration risk.
Unexpected behavior in live operations is a main migration risk.
Incomplete operator readiness is a main migration risk.
Migration mitigation should include validation against real scenarios.
Migration mitigation should include rollback procedures.
Migration mitigation should include training before each release step.
Ongoing maintenance should use a stable support process with careful change control.
Small updates can affect telescope availability and observing efficiency.
The migration shall allow observers to continue working without interruption while the underlying control environment is changed.
The migration shall include a transition plan that preserves current operational procedures as much as possible at first.
The migration shall provide fallback options if something behaves unexpectedly during an observing night.
The migration shall include careful verification of any migrated operational data.
The migration shall include a support path that can respond quickly if the new system affects live observing.
The migration plan shall begin with offline and simulated testing so the team can exercise normal and edge-case observing workflows without touching the telescope.
The migration plan shall include a limited deployment that covers a narrow set of functions or one facility.
During the limited deployment, the old system shall remain available as a backup.
During the limited deployment, the system's behavior shall be compared closely with the old system's behavior.
Full cutover shall occur only after operators are comfortable and the system has proven stable on actual observing nights.
A rollback option shall remain available if something serious comes up.
The system shall complete normal observing tasks reliably.
The system shall have no unresolved defects that affect telescope safety, instrument control, or data quality.
Operators shall be able to run typical sessions confidently.
Operators shall be able to perform handoffs, status checks, and recovery from common faults during typical sessions.
Operators shall be able to complete typical sessions without falling back to the legacy workflow.
The system shall demonstrate stable performance over multiple real observing nights.
The system shall produce clean audit logs and no surprises in shutdown or recovery behavior before moving to the next phase.
The system shall sequence parallel testing first in a non-operational environment.
The system shall support a shadow mode in which the new system observes live activity without taking control.
The system shall allow a limited deployment on a small set of nights or functions only after parallel testing and shadow mode are completed.
The system shall schedule full cutover during a low-risk window.
The system shall keep the legacy system ready as a rollback path until the new system has proven stable for a sustained period.
The system shall implement strong change control as a safeguard.
The system shall provide real-time monitoring.
The system shall give operators clear authority to stop a rollout.
The system shall provide a rapid fallback procedure so unexpected issues do not interrupt an active observation.
